B. METHODS OF SECURING THE JUDGMENT— PROVISIONAL REMEDIES
1.ATTACHMENT
Attachment is a provisional remedy that prevents defendant from selling or otherwise disposing of real or personal property once it
has been taken into custody by the attaching officer. Attachment deprives defendant of the use and enjoyment of property long before
liability is established (and, of course, in many cases no liability will be found). For this reason courts regard it as a drastic remedy and
may decline the request even if statutory requirements are met and plaintiff is willing to post a bond. In particular, the court will consider
the hardship to defendant if the value of the property exceeds the potential liability or if the property is part of an ongoing business.
Attachment is an important provisional remedy when a creditor’s interest is not secured by collateral, which includes the broad range of
contracts for services and material.
NOTES AND QUESTIONS
1. In 1971, relying on Sniadach, the California Supreme Court struck down that state’s prejudgment attachment statute because it permitted seizure

of a debtor’s assets without notice and any hearing upon the filing of an action on an express or implied contract for payment of money. See Randone v.
Appellate Department of the Superior Court of Sacramento County, 5 Cal.3d 536, 96 Cal.Rptr. 709 (1971). The current attachment statute, Cal. Code
of Civil Procedure §§ 481.010 et seq., applies in similar cases when the amount of the claim is fixed or readily ascertainable and not less than $500, and
the amount secured is not less than zero. The applicant must establish “the probable validity” of the claim upon which the attachment is based, which
requires establishing it is more likely than not that a judgment against defendant will be obtained. The amount to be secured may be offset by a claim
against the applicant, provided it is a claim on which an attachment “could be issued.” Id. at § 483.015. In LYDIG CONSTRUCTION, INC. v.
